That feeling quickly turned into curiosity.
I started searching for new signals:
-What metrics actually matter in AI-native companies?
-How are the best operators structuring teams?
-What happens to GTM when AI changes deployment and implementation economics?
-Which roles become more and less valuable?
-Which entirely new roles are emerging? (FDEs, GTM Engineers, AI SDRs)
-What organizational patterns keep repeating at the frontier?

That search turned into hundreds of hours of research:
-40+ executive/operator interviews
-100+ podcast transcripts
-public company examples
-countless notes trying to connect patterns across AI-native companies and traditional software companies trying to transform themselves
Eventually, it led me to build the following “AI-Native Org Design Playbook”.

I do not think the benchmarks or structures in this playbook are copy-paste templates for every tech company.
Why?
-The sample is frontier-skewed.
-Context matters enormously.
-The category is moving incredibly fast — parts of this will probably need rewriting in 6–9 months :)
I see this less as “truth” and more as structured pattern recognition from companies operating close to the edge of the transition.

Inside the playbook:
-GTM-motion-based company segmentation
-function-by-function implications (GTM, product, marketing, CS, hiring, etc.)
-emerging operating-model patterns
-benchmark examples from publicly referenced companies
-interpretations and takeaways from recurring themes across the research

Most importantly, the process genuinely helped me think more clearly in conversations with AI-native founders — and with operators trying to rethink how their companies should evolve in the AI era.
Sharing it publicly in case it becomes useful for others too.

AI agents aren’t ready for the enterprise.

Ardent (YC X26) has been a gamechanger for us developing with AI. 

Have you ever wanted a coding or testing agent to go through your product and figure its own way out, with real data, without messing everything up? 

This company does database branching so that your coding agents and testing agents can work on real or "real" data, do whatever it needs to, and conveniently throws it all away. 

The way it works under the hood is inspired by Neon DB. The short of it is that it has its master copy of your database and tracks only the diffs. Then when you're done with the branch, it throws away all the diffs and it's like nothing ever happened!

posts.content:
T-rex from Greptile is a very interesting indicator of where code validation is going.

A 20% jump in review quality simply from being able to run the code.
This is the same reason "loop engineering" or any recursive coding agent framework works. 

The agent writes code, runs it, sees what breaks, fixes it, runs again. Without the run step the whole loop is just a model guessing at whether its own code works.

Agents need safe environments to test and validate the work they do, and those environments need to be as close to production as possible. Mocks and fixtures drift from reality fast, and an agent validating against data that doesn't match prod is barely validating at all.

We've seen our sandbox volume climb from the tens to the thousands and soon to the hundreds of thousands. That curve is the whole thesis playing out.

As agents do more real work, they need somewhere real to run it, and the demand for production-like environments compounds with every loop they run.
